Chapter 6 · 第六章

Delegating授权与委派

— PDF p.153 —

Delegation is the process of assigning tasks or responsibilities to others while maintaining accountability for the outcome. It means letting go of work that others can take on so you can focus on your main priorities. But delegation is more than just offloading tasks; it's about working as a team, relying on others, and creating opportunities for growth.

授权（delegation）是把任务或职责分派给他人、同时自己仍对最终结果负责的过程。它意味着放下别人能够承担的工作，好让你专注于自己最核心的优先事项。但授权绝不只是把任务甩出去那么简单；它关乎作为一个团队协作、信任他人，并为彼此创造成长的机会。

For example, as a tech lead, you might delegate a feature implementation to a developer instead of coding it yourself. You provide context, set expectations, and offer guidance, but you allow them to own the execution. The key is balancing trust, oversight, and clear communication to ensure success.

举例来说，作为技术负责人，你可以把某个功能的实现授权给一位开发者，而不是自己动手写代码。你提供背景信息、设定期望、给出指导，但让对方真正拥有执行权。关键在于在信任、监督与清晰沟通之间取得平衡，以确保成功。

The reason why delegation is a key skill to master as a tech lead is simple: you can't do everything yourself. Eventually, your workload becomes unsustainable. Your role shifts from being a great individual contributor to enabling your team to succeed. The most effective tech leads aren't the ones who take on every critical task themselves; they're the ones who build strong, autonomous teams that can execute effectively without micromanagement.

授权之所以是技术负责人必须掌握的关键技能，原因很简单：你不可能事事亲为。终有一天，你的工作量会变得难以为继。你的角色会从一名出色的个人贡献者，转变为赋能团队取得成功的人。最有成效的技术负责人，不是那些把每一项关键任务都揽在自己身上的人，而是那些打造出强大、自主、无需微观管理就能高效执行的团队的人。

Despite its importance, delegation is one of the hardest skills for tech leads to develop. Many struggle with it, often hesitating because they fear losing control, worry about the outcome, or feel like it's faster to just do it themselves. Some even hold back because they fear they won't get the credit for work they delegate.

尽管授权如此重要，它却是技术负责人最难培养的技能之一。很多人都为此挣扎，常常犹豫不决：害怕失去控制、担心结果不如人意，或者觉得自己动手反而更快。有些人甚至因为担心授权出去的工作功劳落不到自己头上而退缩。

That's why this chapter is structured to cover everything you need to know to delegate effectively and with confidence:

正因如此，本章的结构安排会覆盖你所需了解的一切，帮你高效而自信地完成授权：

  • The benefits of delegation: how it helps you gain back time, grow your team (and yourself), and improve overall team performance.授权的益处：它如何帮你赢回时间、培养团队（以及你自己），并提升团队的整体绩效。
— PDF p.154 —
  • A step-by-step guide to delegation, from deciding what to delegate and who to delegate to, to choosing the right delegation strategy, setting clear expectations, and following up.一份循序渐进的授权指南：从决定授权什么、授权给谁，到选择恰当的授权策略、设定清晰的期望，以及后续跟进。
  • The four most common fears tech leads face when delegating and how to overcome them.技术负责人在授权时最常见的四种恐惧，以及如何克服它们。

By the end of this chapter, you'll have the tools to delegate with confidence, scale your impact as a leader, and build a stronger, more self-reliant team.

读完本章，你将掌握一套工具，让你自信地授权、放大作为领导者的影响力，并打造一支更强大、更自立的团队。

Benefits of Delegation授权的益处

Delegation is one of the most underrated yet powerful skills a tech lead can develop.

授权是技术负责人所能培养的、最被低估却也最强大的技能之一。

When done right, delegation frees up your time to focus on high-impact work while also empowering your team members by giving them ownership and growth opportunities. Over time, this leads to a team that runs more efficiently, makes better decisions, and requires less hands-on oversight from you.

如果做得得当，授权能把你的时间解放出来，去专注高影响力的工作；同时，通过赋予团队成员主人翁感和成长机会，他们也得到赋能。久而久之，团队运转会更高效、决策更明智，也越来越不需要你事必躬亲地盯着。

Each of these outcomes is worth unpacking on its own, so let's look more closely at the core benefits of delegation and how they show up in your day-to-day work as a tech lead.

这些结果每一个都值得单独展开来讲。下面我们就更细致地看看授权的核心益处，以及它们如何体现在你作为技术负责人的日常工作中。

Gaining Time for You为自己赢得时间

One of the biggest struggles tech leads bring to me in coaching is time management. They feel constantly overwhelmed, juggling too many responsibilities: coding, one-on-ones, alignment meetings, firefighting, and performance reviews while still feeling like they're never doing enough. There's always something important that gets pushed aside. They end up chasing their day, moving from one thing to another without ever feeling in control.

在教练辅导中，技术负责人向我倾诉的最大困扰之一就是时间管理。他们总觉得不堪重负，同时应付太多职责：写代码、一对一沟通、对齐会议、救火、绩效评估，却仍觉得自己做得远远不够。总有一些重要的事被推到一边。最终他们只能被日子追着跑，从一件事扑到另一件事，却从未真正拥有掌控感。

Delegation is one of the most effective ways to offload some of these tasks and win back time.

授权是卸下这些任务、赢回时间最有效的方式之一。

When working with overwhelmed tech leads, the first thing I do is analyze their workload. We look at what's on their plate and identify tasks that don't require their direct involvement, tasks that could be handled by others in the team. The goal is to redistribute their responsibilities effectively. Once we identify what to delegate, the next step is making it happen (more on that in the section "Delegation Process: Step-by-Step" on page 143).

和不堪重负的技术负责人合作时，我做的第一件事就是分析他们的工作量。我们一起看他们肩上都有什么，找出那些不需要他们亲自介入、可以交给团队其他人处理的任务。目标是有效地重新分配他们的职责。一旦确定了该授权什么，下一步就是付诸行动（更多内容见第 143 页"授权流程：一步一步来"一节）。

— PDF p.155 —

A classic example I see all the time: a technical, repetitive task that only the tech lead knows how to do. Maybe it's for an important client, and it involves a system or service that no one else fully understands. It's a 30-minute task every week. Easy, routine, predictable. You could do it with your eyes closed. You even do the task on vacation because, well, it's just easier to do it yourself. You've been meaning to automate it or, at the very least, document the steps to do it, but there's always something more urgent.

我经常看到一个典型例子：一项技术性、重复性的任务，只有技术负责人自己知道怎么做。也许是为某个重要客户做的，涉及一个其他人都不完全理解的系统或服务。这是一项每周一次、每次 30 分钟的任务。简单、例行、可预测。你闭着眼睛都能做。你甚至在度假时也在做这件事，因为——唉，自己动手就是更省事。你一直想把它自动化，或者至少把操作步骤写下来，但总有更紧急的事插进来。

There are multiple problems with this approach. Besides wasting your time on something that could easily be delegated, you're creating a knowledge silo and increasing your team's bus factor risk. If you're suddenly unavailable, whether due to illness, an emergency, or simply being on leave, no one else can step in. Your team depends on you for this task, and no one else gets the opportunity to learn it.

这种做法有很多问题。除了把你的时间浪费在一件本可以轻松授权出去的事上，你还在制造知识孤岛，并抬高团队的"巴士因子"风险。万一你突然没空——无论是生病、突发状况，还是单纯在休假——没有任何人能顶上来。团队在这件事上依赖你，而其他人也永远得不到学习它的机会。

Now imagine delegating it, not just passing the task on but giving someone else ownership of it, including finding a way to automate it. Yes, it might take some effort up front to train them, but the payoff in the long run is that you can remove it from your to-do list.

现在想象一下把它授权出去：不只是把任务转手，而是让另一个人真正拥有它，包括去想办法把它自动化。没错，前期培训他们确实要花些力气，但长期回报是——你可以把它从自己的待办清单上彻底划掉。

These "quick" 30-minute tasks are the real silent killers of your time. It's never just about the time spent doing them; it's about the impact of context switching. Studies show that it takes around 23 minutes to fully regain focus after being distracted. So those "easy" tasks might be stealing more of your time than you realize.

这些"很快"的 30 分钟小任务，才是你时间真正的沉默杀手。问题从来不只是做它们花掉的那点时间，而是上下文切换带来的冲击。研究表明，人在被打断后，大约需要 23 分钟才能重新完全集中注意力。所以那些"简单"的任务，偷走的时间可能比你以为的要多得多。

Letting go of some things on your plate doesn't mean you're doing less; it means you're focusing on what really needs your attention as a tech lead—the things only you can do.

把肩上的一些事放下，并不意味着你做得更少；而是意味着你把精力聚焦到作为技术负责人真正需要你关注的事上——那些只有你能做的事。

By delegating effectively, you take back control of your time. You can finally plan your work, make space for strategic thinking, and stop feeling like you're constantly playing catch-up.

通过高效授权，你重新夺回对时间的掌控。你终于可以规划自己的工作，为战略思考留出空间，不再总觉得自己在疲于追赶。

Helping Your Team (and Yourself) Grow帮助团队（也帮助自己）成长

Besides freeing up your time, delegation is also one of the most powerful ways to help your team grow and build confidence.

除了解放你的时间，授权也是帮助团队成长、建立自信最有力的方式之一。

One of the most common traps tech leads fall into (especially in smaller teams) is trying to stay on top of everything. They want to know the status of every feature, make sure everything is moving forward, and be involved in every decision. But this approach quickly becomes unsustainable.

技术负责人最常掉进的陷阱之一（尤其是在小团队里），就是试图事事都亲自掌握。他们想知道每个功能的状态、确保一切都在推进、并参与每一个决策。但这种做法很快就会难以为继。

A strategy that completely changed the way I worked at Thoughtworks was assigning feature leads. Instead of keeping everything on my plate, each feature had an owner. That meant another developer, not me, was responsible for making sure there was a clear plan, ensuring the team was aligned, tracking dependencies, creating stories, making progress visible, and identifying risks

在 Thoughtworks，有一个策略彻底改变了我的工作方式：为每个功能指定负责人。我不再把所有事都扛在自己身上，而是让每个功能都有一个 owner。这意味着由另一位开发者（而不是我）来负责：确保有清晰的计划、团队保持对齐、追踪依赖、创建用户故事、让进展可见，并及早识别风险——

— PDF p.156 —

early. Their job wasn't to do all the work alone but to own the process, involve the team, and escalate issues when needed.

他们的工作不是独自干完所有事，而是拥有整个过程、让团队参与进来，并在必要时把问题升级上报。

My involvement dropped significantly. I was still accountable for the outcome and needed to stay informed, but I no longer had to micromanage every step. Depending on the feature, I even encouraged them to handle stakeholder updates themselves. That way, they had full autonomy, and I stepped in only if something went wrong.

我的介入大幅减少。我仍然对结果负责，也需要保持知情，但不再去微观管理每一个步骤。视功能而定，我甚至鼓励他们自己去处理与干系人的同步沟通。这样一来，他们拥有完全的自主权，而我只在出问题时才介入。

As they took on these new responsibilities, I could see them testing out leadership skills, managing complexity, communicating across roles, and making trade-offs, all in a safe, supported environment. These opportunities built not just their technical confidence but their leadership capabilities.

当他们承担起这些新职责时，我能看到他们在一个安全、有支持的环境里，尝试着锻炼领导力技能、管理复杂性、跨角色沟通，并做出权衡取舍。这些机会不仅建立了他们的技术自信，也培养了他们的领导能力。

At the same time, what I didn't expect was that I often learned more from the process than they did. There's a saying that you don't truly know something until you explain it to someone else. The longer you do things a certain way, the less you question them. But when you hand a task over to someone new, suddenly, they start asking all the right questions. "Why do we do it like this?" "What if we changed that?" "Could this be improved?" Delegating opened the door to fresh ideas, challenges to the status quo, and improvements I never would have thought of. I was able to help others grow, and I was pushed to grow as well. Letting go means being open to the idea that your way might not always be the best way. And people will surprise you, if you give them the chance.

与此同时，我没料到的是：在这个过程中，我学到的往往比他们还多。有句话说，你只有把一件事讲给别人听，才算真正懂了它。一件事按某种方式做得越久，你就越不去质疑它。但当你把一个任务交给一个新人时，他们突然会问出一堆恰到好处的问题："我们为什么要这样做？""如果把那一点改了会怎样？""这里能不能改进？"授权为新鲜想法、对现状的挑战、以及我从未想到过的改进打开了大门。我在帮助别人成长的同时，也被推着成长。放下，意味着愿意接受这样一种可能：你的方式未必永远是最好的方式。而只要给人们机会，他们往往会让你惊喜。

Delegation works best when it's rooted in trust. It's about giving people opportunities to grow and making sure the entire team shares the responsibility of delivering work. And the best way to build confidence in someone is to tell them: "I trust you to handle this." This single sentence can completely change how someone sees themselves.

当授权植根于信任时，效果最好。它是给人们成长的机会，并确保交付工作的责任由整个团队共同承担。而建立一个人自信的最佳方式，就是告诉他："我相信你能处理好这件事。"单单这一句话，就能彻底改变一个人对自己的看法。

Delegation gives others space to step up, experiment, and learn while also helping you grow as a leader who empowers rather than controls. If you want to build a strong, resilient team, learning to let go, strategically and supportively, is one of the most effective things you can do.

授权给他人留出站出来、尝试和学习的空间，同时也帮助你成长为一个赋能型、而非控制型的领导者。如果你想打造一支强大、有韧性的团队，那么学会有策略、有支持地放手，就是你能做的最有效的事情之一。

Boosting Team Performance提升团队绩效

Beyond individual growth, delegation also strengthens the team as a whole. As more team members step into ownership, the team becomes more collaborative, resilient, and efficient. People start supporting one another, spotting gaps, sharing knowledge, and solving problems together. Instead of relying on a single point of decision making, they learn to move forward confidently as a group. This shift positively impacts the overall performance of the team.

除了个人成长，授权还能让整个团队变得更强。当越来越多的团队成员站出来承担主人翁责任时，团队会变得更协作、更有韧性、更高效。人们开始互相支持、发现缺口、分享知识、共同解决问题。他们不再依赖单一的决策点，而是学会作为一个整体自信地向前推进。这一转变会积极地影响团队的整体绩效。

— PDF p.157 —

A great example of this is handling technical interviews. I worked with a tech lead who believed she needed to be involved in every single interview to ensure quality hires. She spent hours reviewing resumes, conducting coding assessments, and leading debriefs. While hiring is undeniably important, this level of involvement drained her time and slowed down the hiring process.

一个很好的例子是处理技术面试。我曾和一位技术负责人合作，她认为自己必须参与每一场面试，才能保证招到合适的人。她花大量时间筛选简历、组织编码测评、主持复盘。招聘固然极其重要，但这种程度的亲自参与耗尽了她的时间，也拖慢了招聘流程。

We worked on a plan: instead of being the bottleneck, she trained senior engineers to take over key parts of the hiring pipeline. She created a structured rubric for technical evaluations, standardized interview questions, and a clear debriefing process. Over time, she stepped in only when absolutely necessary. As a result, the team fully owned the process, and the overall performance of both the hiring process and the team improved dramatically:

我们一起制定了一个计划：她不再做瓶颈，而是培训资深工程师接手招聘流程中的关键环节。她制定了结构化的技术评估评分表、标准化的面试题，以及清晰的复盘流程。久而久之，她只在绝对必要时才介入。结果是：团队完全拥有了这个流程，招聘流程和团队双方的整体绩效都大幅提升：

  • The hiring process moved faster because it no longer relied on just one person. The team could conduct multiple interviews simultaneously, keeping the pipeline flowing.招聘流程更快了，因为它不再只依赖一个人。团队可以同时进行多场面试，让招聘管道保持畅通。
  • Team members had a say in who joined, increasing alignment between new hires and the existing culture.团队成员对谁能加入有了发言权，提升了新员工与现有文化之间的契合度。
  • Everyone learned something. Some engineers developed interviewing skills, while the tech lead gained insight into hiring bottlenecks and how to avoid them in the future.每个人都学到了东西。一些工程师锻炼了面试技能，而技术负责人则更清楚招聘瓶颈在哪里、未来该如何避免。
  • Onboarding time was reduced. With more time freed up, the tech lead could focus on refining the onboarding process, ensuring new hires could contribute faster and more effectively.新人入职上手的时间缩短了。有了更多空出来的时间，技术负责人可以专注于优化入职流程，确保新员工更快、更高效地做出贡献。

A high-performing team is one that functions well even when you're not around. A big part of being a tech lead is helping the team get there. That means taking what's in your head and sharing it with others.

一支高绩效团队，是那种即便你不在场也能良好运转的团队。作为技术负责人，很重要的一部分工作就是帮团队抵达这种状态。这意味着把你脑子里的东西拿出来，分享给其他人。

One of the biggest blockers I see in tech teams is work that isn't ready to be worked on. People end up sitting around because the next tasks aren't refined enough. The natural reaction is that the tech lead and product manager take over pre-refinement, preparing stories in advance so the team can keep moving. It works but only for a while. Eventually, it becomes another bottleneck, another task weighing you down.

我在技术团队里看到的最大阻塞之一，就是"还没准备好开工"的工作。人们最后只能干坐着，因为接下来的任务细化得不够。自然而然的反应是：技术负责人和产品经理接手预细化，提前把用户故事准备好，好让团队继续往前走。这办法有效，但只能管一阵子。最终，它又变成一个瓶颈、又一项压在你身上的任务。

In my team, we made pre-refinement a shared responsibility. Instead of me always working with the product manager to prepare upcoming work, everyone took turns. It became part of the team's weekly work, ensuring that when sprint

在我的团队里，我们把预细化变成了一项共同责任。不再总是由我和产品经理两人去准备接下来的工作，而是大家轮流承担。它成了团队每周工作的一部分，确保当冲刺

— PDF p.158 —

planning came around, stories were ready to go. No one was left waiting, and I wasn't scrambling to do it all.

评审会到来时，用户故事已经准备就绪。没有人干等着，我也不必手忙脚乱地一个人包揽。

But of course, getting there was a journey. It didn't happen overnight.

当然，走到这一步是一段旅程，并非一夜之间发生。

We started by laying the groundwork. We defined a clear structure for user stories, including consistent formatting, required context, and clearly written acceptance criteria. That gave everyone a shared understanding of what "ready" looked like.

我们从打基础开始。我们为用户故事定义了清晰的结构，包括统一的格式、必要的背景信息，以及写得清楚的验收标准。这让每个人对"什么叫准备好了"有了共同的理解。

We also leaned into pair programming, but not randomly. We put more thought into how we formed pairs for pre-refinement. One person would bring the technical context, while the other might be newer to the feature or to refinement itself or have less experience. That way, the task got done well, and someone also learned in the process.

我们还借助结对编程，但不是随便配对。我们在如何为预细化结对这件事上花了更多心思。一个人带来技术背景，另一个人可能对这个功能、对细化工作本身还比较新，或经验较少。这样一来，任务既能高质量完成，也有人在过程中学到了东西。

Before anything was brought in front of stakeholders or the product manager, we would often run pre-refinement discussions as a team, diving into technical considerations and edge cases together. The goal of these conversations was getting stories ready and building shared ownership and technical judgment.

在任何东西被拿到干系人或产品经理面前之前，我们常常作为一个团队先开预细化讨论会，一起深入探讨技术考量和边界情况。这些对话的目标，是把用户故事准备好，并建立共同的主人翁意识和技术判断力。

With time, people got the hang of it. The structure, pairing, and shared discussions gave everyone the tools they needed to contribute meaningfully. And as their confidence grew, my involvement became less and less.

随着时间推移，大家慢慢上手了。这套结构、结对和共同讨论，给了每个人做出有意义贡献所需的工具。而随着他们信心的增长，我的介入也越来越少。

Delegation means investing in your team's growth so you can step back, knowing things will still run smoothly. And someone not being ready yet is not a reason to avoid delegating; rather, it's your invitation to start preparing them.

授权意味着投资于团队的成长，好让你能够退一步，并且知道事情依然会顺畅运转。而某人"还没准备好"，绝不是回避授权的理由；恰恰相反，它是在邀请你开始培养他。

By sharing knowledge and responsibility, you remove yourself as a bottleneck and enable your team to function independently. A good test of healthy delegation is this: can you take a real two-week vacation without needing to check in constantly? If the answer is yes, you've done it right.

通过分享知识和责任，你把自己从瓶颈的位置上撤下来，让团队能够独立运转。检验授权是否健康的一个好标准是：你能不能真正休一次两周的假，而不需要不断地远程查岗？如果答案是肯定的，那你就做对了。

Of course, you might argue that teaching others to take over tasks slows the team down in the short term. And that's true, at first. But in the long run, your team becomes more autonomous, less dependent on you, and better equipped to move faster and more efficiently without unnecessary blockers. Less time wasted waiting for you. More time for you to focus on what only you can do.

当然，你也许会说，教别人接手任务在短期内会拖慢团队。没错，一开始确实如此。但从长远看，团队会变得更自主、更不依赖你，也更有能力在没有不必要阻塞的情况下更快、更高效地推进。花在等你身上的时间更少了。你也有更多时间去专注那些只有你能做的事。

As a tech lead, you're always playing the long game. Delegation is how you win it.

作为技术负责人，你永远在打一场长线的游戏。而授权，就是你赢得这场游戏的方式。

— PDF p.159 —

Delegation Process: Step-by-Step授权流程：一步一步来

Now that I've covered why delegation is essential and the countless benefits it brings, like gaining back your time, growing your team, reducing bottlenecks, and ultimately improving team performance, let's move on to the how.

既然我已经讲清了授权为何必不可少，以及它带来的诸多益处——赢回时间、培养团队、减少瓶颈，并最终提升团队绩效，下面我们就来谈谈"怎么做"。

Delegating is about making sure the right people are handling the right tasks in a way that benefits both them and the team. When done right, it builds confidence, distributes workload effectively, and helps the team operate smoothly, even without you overseeing everything. But if done without care, it can create confusion, frustration, and more problems than it solves.

授权，就是确保合适的人以一种对他们自己和团队都有利的方式去处理合适的任务。做得好，它能建立自信、有效分配工作量，并帮助团队在你不事事盯着的情况下依然顺畅运转。但如果漫不经心地做，它会制造混乱、挫败感，带来的问题甚至比解决的还多。

Some tech leads struggle more with certain aspects of delegation than others. Maybe you find it hard to decide what to delegate. Maybe you're unsure who should take on a task or you're worried the outcome won't meet your expectations. That's why breaking down the process step-by-step is so important.

有些技术负责人在授权的某些环节上挣扎得更厉害。也许你觉得很难决定该授权什么。也许你拿不准该让谁来接，或者担心结果达不到你的期望。正因如此，把整个流程一步一步拆解开来才如此重要。

In this section, I'll go deep into each step of effective delegation: identifying the right tasks, choosing the right person and the right delegation strategy, and setting clear expectations, all while maintaining accountability.

在本节中，我会深入讲解高效授权的每一步：识别合适的任务、选对合适的人和恰当的授权策略、设定清晰的期望，同时始终保持担责。

What to Delegate该授权什么

Many tech leads struggle with feeling like they need to do everything themselves when, in reality, the opposite is true. The first step to effective delegation is figuring out what can be handed off, something that a lot of tech leads find surprisingly difficult. It often feels like everything they do is essential, but that's rarely the case.

许多技术负责人都有一种"必须事事亲为"的感觉，而现实恰恰相反。高效授权的第一步，是弄清楚哪些事可以交出去——很多技术负责人发现这件事出奇地难。他们往往觉得自己做的每一件事都至关重要，但事实很少如此。

A simple exercise to start is this: at the end of the week, write down all the tasks you handled. Then analyze: what are the things only you can do? This might include holding one-on-ones with stakeholders, defining the technical strategy for a company-wide cloud migration, refining technical stories with the product manager, or running performance reviews. These are tasks that often require your insight and full attention. Everything else is potentially delegatable.

一个可以立刻开始的简单练习是：在周末，把你这一周处理过的所有任务都写下来。然后分析：哪些事是只有你能做的？这可能包括与干系人开一对一、为全公司范围的云迁移制定技术战略、和产品经理一起细化技术用户故事，或主持绩效评估。这些任务往往需要你的判断力和全身心投入。除此之外的一切，原则上都可以授权。

And honestly, even those high-level tasks like defining the technical strategy for a company-wide cloud migration don't always need to be yours. Another developer on your team should be able to step into some of those conversations over time. And likewise, you can share the responsibility of refining technical stories with the whole team. If your absence causes a roadblock, then you've become a bottleneck. What happens when you're not around? Why can't someone else take over? The reality is, in many companies, tech leads are expected to be the

而且说实话，即便是那些高层次任务——比如为全公司云迁移制定技术战略——也未必永远得由你来做。随着时间推移，团队里另一位开发者应该能够走进其中一些讨论。同样，你也可以把细化技术用户故事的责任分享给整个团队。如果你的缺席会造成阻塞，那你就已经变成了瓶颈。你不在的时候会发生什么？为什么不能由别人来接手？现实是，在很多公司，技术负责人被期待成为

— PDF p.160 —

go-to for everything, but that doesn't mean it has to stay that way.

事事都找的那个人，但这并不意味着它必须一直如此。

Start small. Delegating simpler, repetitive tasks first will help you get comfortable with the process while showing your team you trust them. You can delegate both technical and nontechnical tasks, as you'll see in the coming examples.

从小处着手。先把较简单、重复的任务授权出去，会帮你慢慢适应这个过程，同时向团队表明你信任他们。你既可以授权技术性任务，也可以授权非技术性任务，后面的例子你会看到这一点。

Another great category of tasks to delegate are tasks you don't want to do. That might sound selfish at first, but often these are tasks you've simply outgrown. Just because you find something tedious doesn't mean someone else on the team won't see it as a great learning opportunity. What's routine for you might be new and exciting for them, and a great opportunity to develop new skills.

另一类非常适合授权的任务，是那些你自己不想做的事。乍听这也许有点自私，但通常这些只是你早已"长大毕业"的任务。你觉得某件事乏味，并不意味着团队里另一个人不会把它看作一个绝佳的学习机会。对你来说稀松平常的事，对他们可能新鲜而令人兴奋，是锻炼新技能的好机会。

Onboarding new engineers is also a great example of a delegatable task. Many tech leads take full ownership of onboarding, walking every new hire through documentation, setting up their local environment, and explaining company processes. While it's important to ensure new team members are set up for success, this entire process doesn't have to be done by you.

让新工程师入职，也是一个非常典型的可授权任务。许多技术负责人把新人入职全程揽在自己身上：带每一位新员工过文档、帮他们配置本地环境、讲解公司流程。虽然确保新成员开好局很重要，但这整套流程并不非得由你亲手完成。

Instead, create an onboarding buddy system where a senior or mid-level engineer takes responsibility for guiding new hires through their first few weeks. They can help with setup, answer questions, and provide technical context. You can still check in at key points, but by delegating the hands-on part, you ensure new hires get support while freeing yourself up for higher-level tasks. Plus, it's a great leadership development opportunity for the buddy. (For a deeper dive into how to set up an effective onboarding system, see the section "Onboarding Effectively" on page 175.)

不妨建立一套"入职伙伴（buddy）"制度：由一位资深或中级工程师负责在最初几周引导新员工。他们可以帮忙搭环境、解答问题、提供技术背景。你仍然可以在关键节点上跟进，但通过把实操部分授权出去，你既保证了新员工得到支持，又把自己解放出来去做更高层次的事。此外，这对那位 buddy 来说也是一次绝佳的领导力培养机会。（关于如何搭建一套高效的入职体系，详见第 175 页"高效入职"一节。）

Meetings are another easy win. I worked with a client whose company had recurring guild meetings on architecture, frontend solutions, and other topics. Instead of attending all of them, I found team members interested in those areas and had them go instead. Their job was to attend the meetings consistently, bring back insights, and flag anything that might impact our team. The outcome was highly effective: it saved me time, kept the team informed, and gave those team members a sense of ownership and visibility across the organization. It also created learning opportunities and helped them build internal networks. On top of that, by ensuring someone always showed up, we demonstrated to our client that we prioritized these conversations and cared about cross-team collaboration, without it always having to come from me.

会议是另一项轻松的胜利。我曾服务过一位客户，其公司有关于架构、前端方案等主题的定期"行会（guild）"会议。我没有每场都自己去，而是找团队里对这些领域感兴趣的成员，让他们替我参加。他们的职责是：持续出席会议、带回见解、并标出任何可能影响我们团队的事项。结果非常有效：既省了我的时间，又让团队保持知情，还让这些成员在整个组织中拥有了主人翁感和可见度。它还创造了学习机会，帮他们建立起内部人脉。更重要的是，通过保证总有我们的人到场，我们向客户表明我们重视这些讨论、在意跨团队协作，而不必每次都由我亲自出面。

If you're unsure where to start, the Eisenhower Matrix is a great tool to categorize your workload (check out the section "Time Management" on page 45 for details). It helps you separate what's truly urgent and important from what can be delegated, postponed, or dropped entirely.

如果你不确定从何下手，艾森豪威尔矩阵是一个很好用的工具，可以帮你对工作量分类（详见第 45 页"时间管理"一节）。它能帮你把真正紧急且重要的事，与那些可以授权、推迟或干脆放弃的事区分开来。

— PDF p.161 —

And if you want even more ideas, ask your team. One-on-ones are a perfect space for this. Try: "Is there anything I'm doing that you'd be interested in taking over?" You'd be surprised at the answers you get if you just ask.

如果你还想要更多点子，那就去问你的团队。一对一正是问这个的完美场合。不妨试试："我现在做的事情里，有没有哪件是你有兴趣接手的？"只要开口问，你会惊讶于得到的回答。

These are just some ideas to get you started. Once you begin thinking more intentionally about delegation, you'll find even more opportunities to free up your time while empowering your team.

这些只是帮你入门的一些点子。一旦你开始更有意识地思考授权，就会发现更多既能解放时间、又能赋能团队的机会。

Who to Delegate To授权给谁

Once you know what to delegate, the next step is figuring out who should take it on. The goal is to balance team growth, workload, and efficiency. Choose someone who not only has the capability but is also in a position to benefit from the opportunity. The right match leads to a smooth handoff. Otherwise, the task may end up right back on your plate.

一旦确定了该授权什么，下一步就是弄清楚该让谁来接。目标是在团队成长、工作量和效率之间取得平衡。要选一个既有能力、又能从这次机会中获益的人。匹配得当，交接就会顺畅；否则，这项任务最后可能又落回你的肩上。

The following sections cover some things to consider when choosing the person to delegate to.

下面几节会讲讲在挑选授权对象时需要考虑的一些因素。

Who is interested?谁有兴趣？

Motivation often matters more than prior experience. Someone eager to learn will put in the effort to get up to speed quickly. Instead of assuming who might be interested, ask.

动机往往比过往经验更重要。一个渴望学习的人，会主动下功夫快速上手。不要自己猜谁可能感兴趣，去问。

For example, a tech lead I worked with always was the one to run sprint demos or showcases. I encouraged him to delegate the responsibility to different team members on a rotating basis by simply saying in a standup, "I usually run the sprint demo, but I'd love for someone else to take the lead this time. Who's interested?"

举例来说，我合作过的一位技术负责人，一直是由他本人来主持冲刺演示或成果展示。我鼓励他把这项责任轮流授权给不同的团队成员，做法很简单——在站会上说一句："冲刺演示往常都是我来主持，但这一次我很希望由别人来牵头。谁有兴趣？"

This not only distributes the workload but also helps developers improve their presentation skills, gain visibility, and build confidence in communicating with stakeholders. It also supports inclusion by creating visible opportunities that more junior or underrepresented team members can step into—opportunities they might not have asked for otherwise.

这不仅分摊了工作量，还帮开发者锻炼了演讲能力、获得了可见度，并在与干系人沟通时建立自信。它也促进了包容：创造出可见的机会，让更初级、或平时话语权不足的成员也能站出来承担——这些机会，他们原本可能根本不会开口去争取。

If more than one person expresses interest, that's a great sign. You can rotate the responsibility across people, pair them up, or take into account the criteria that follow, like skill fit or availability, to decide who takes the lead this time. Either way, interest is a strong signal that's worth nurturing.

如果不止一个人表示感兴趣，那是个好兆头。你可以让大家轮流承担、把他们结对，或结合接下来要讲的标准（比如技能匹配度或手头是否有空）来决定这次由谁牵头。无论如何，兴趣都是一个值得悉心培育的强烈信号。

One-on-ones are also a great space to identify interest. If you notice a team member looking to grow in a specific area, you can frame it like this: "I usually handle [task], but I think this could be a great learning opportunity for you. Want to pair on it this time?"

一对一也是发现兴趣的好场合。如果你注意到某位团队成员想在某个特定方向成长，你可以这样开口："[某任务]往常都是我来处理，但我觉得这对你会是个很好的学习机会。这次要不要和我一起做？"

— PDF p.162 —

Who has the knowledge?谁具备相关知识？

How urgent or high-impact is the task? If something needs to be done quickly and correctly with minimal support, delegate it to someone who already has the knowledge.

这项任务有多紧急、多高影响？如果某件事需要在最少支持下又快又准地完成，那就把它授权给已经具备相关知识的人。

If no one else on the team can do it, it means you are a bottleneck. Start by pairing with someone. Have them document the process and try replicating the task when there's no pressure. Next time, let them take the wheel while you stay in the background for support.

如果团队里没有第二个人能做，那就意味着你自己成了瓶颈。先从和某人结对开始。让他把流程记录下来，并在没有压力的时候试着复现这项任务。下一次，让他来掌舵，你退到幕后提供支持。

For example, a tech lead was responsible for setting up CI/CD pipelines for every new microservice. It was slowing him down, and the team relied on him as the only person who understood the setup. Instead of being a bottleneck, he paired with another engineer, documented the steps, and let them handle the setup for the next service. Eventually, multiple people could set up pipelines, reducing dependency on him.

举例来说，有一位技术负责人负责为每个新的微服务搭建 CI/CD 流水线。这件事拖慢了他，而团队也把他当成唯一懂这套配置的人来依赖。他没有继续做瓶颈，而是和另一位工程师结对、把步骤写下来，并让对方去处理下一个服务的搭建。最终，多个人都能搭建流水线了，对他的依赖随之降低。

If working remotely and both agree, you could even record the pairing session or create a quick screencast walkthrough. It's a lightweight, low-lift way to capture the knowledge transfer and helps the person reviewing the task later to document the process more thoroughly. It becomes a reusable reference for the whole team.

如果是远程办公、且双方都同意，你甚至可以录下结对过程，或做一个简短的屏幕录制讲解。这是一种轻量、低成本的方式，既留存了知识传递，也帮之后接手这项任务的人把流程记录得更完整。它会成为整个团队可复用的参考资料。

Be careful not to always choose the most qualified person. This can create knowledge silos or overwhelm certain team members while others miss learning opportunities. For low-risk tasks with no urgent deadline, give them to someone who wants to build experience in that area. Yes, it might take longer the first time, but in the long run, it distributes knowledge across the team.

要注意不要总是选那个最资深的人。这样会造成知识孤岛，或让某些成员不堪重负，而另一些人却错失学习机会。对于低风险、又没有紧急截止日期的任务，把它交给那个想在该领域积累经验的人。没错，第一次可能会慢一些，但从长远看，它把知识散布到了整个团队。

What's their current workload?他们当前的工作量如何？

Delegation is meant to reduce your workload, not just shift it onto someone else. Before assigning a task, check in with them. Some team members might say yes to everything because they see it as a privilege, but they may already be overloaded. Ask directly: "How would this fit into your workload right now?" instead of assuming that it does.

授权的本意是减轻你的工作量，而不只是把它转嫁到别人身上。在分派任务之前，先和对方确认一下。有些团队成员可能对什么都答应，因为他们把这看作一种认可，但他们也许早已超负荷。直接问一句："这件事放在你现在的工作量里，合适吗？"而不是想当然地认为没问题。

A common pitfall I've seen is tech leads always delegating to the same person. One tech lead always relied on a senior engineer for documentation-heavy tasks like writing architecture decision records (ADRs). After a while, the engineer got frustrated and asked why no one else was responsible for it. The tech lead realized that she hadn't considered workload balance and started rotating this responsibility, giving others a chance to develop that skill.

我见过一个常见的坑：技术负责人总是授权给同一个人。有位技术负责人，凡是像撰写架构决策记录（ADR）这类文档量大的任务，总是依赖同一位资深工程师。一段时间后，这位工程师很沮丧，问为什么这件事没有别人来负责。技术负责人这才意识到自己没考虑工作量平衡，于是开始轮流承担这项责任，让其他人也有机会锻炼这项技能。

— PDF p.163 —

Does their working style match the task?他们的工作风格与任务匹配吗？

The right person isn't always the most experienced; it depends on the nature of the task.

合适的人未必总是经验最丰富的那个；这取决于任务的性质。

If you need someone to own communication and alignment between teams on a high-impact project, pick someone who enjoys collaboration and has strong soft skills.

如果你需要有人在一个高影响项目上负责跨团队的沟通与对齐，那就选一个喜欢协作、软技能强的人。

If you're trying to debug a complex memory leak, delegate it to someone who thrives on technical deep dives and enjoys solving intricate problems.

如果你要调试一个复杂的内存泄漏，那就把它授权给那种以技术深挖为乐、享受解决错综复杂问题的人。

If you're unsure how to spot these traits in your team, you're not alone. It takes time to develop this skill. A good first step is simply paying attention to how people behave in different situations.

如果你不确定如何在团队中识别这些特质，你并不孤单。这项技能需要时间来培养。很好的第一步，就是留心观察人们在不同情境下的行为方式。

For example, someone who's a strong communicator often volunteers to clarify points in meetings, follows up in writing, facilitates retrospectives, and checks in with team members to keep everyone aligned. They tend to be proactive, taking on extra responsibilities, stepping up to lead initiatives, and looking for ways to be involved in broader conversations.

例如，一个擅长沟通的人，常常会主动在会议上澄清要点、以书面形式跟进、主持回顾会，并主动和团队成员对齐以保持大家步调一致。他们往往很主动，愿意承担额外责任、站出来牵头各项议题，并寻找机会参与到更广泛的讨论中。

In contrast, someone who thrives on deep technical work might light up when tackling complex problems, eagerly jump into debugging, or take the lead during incidents. They're often the ones suggesting technical improvements or exploring new tools and approaches.

与之相对，一个以深度技术工作为乐的人，可能在攻克复杂问题时两眼放光、热切地投入调试，或在故障期间挺身而出牵头处理。他们常常是那些提出技术改进建议、或探索新工具与新方法的人。

Pay attention to what energizes each person, what they naturally take ownership of, and how they engage with others. These patterns can give you valuable insight into their strengths.

留意是什么让每个人充满干劲、他们自然而然会把哪些事揽在自己身上，以及他们如何与他人互动。这些行为模式，能让你宝贵地洞察他们的长处。

Of course, this doesn't mean the task always needs to match their current style. Delegation can be a great growth opportunity. Sometimes it's worth giving a strong IC a chance to lead a cross-team initiative or asking a great communicator to dive deeper into technical ownership. These mismatches can challenge people to build new muscles and grow in unexpected ways, especially when they have deep expertise in a certain area and can bring unique value to the task.

当然，这并不意味着任务永远要和他们当下的风格相吻合。授权本身也可以是一次很好的成长机会。有时，值得让一个很强的 IC 有机会牵头一个跨团队议题，或请一个优秀的沟通者更深入地承担技术上的主人翁责任。这种"错配"会挑战人们锻炼新的能力，以意想不到的方式成长——尤其是当他们在某个领域有深厚专长、能为任务带来独特价值时。

These are not a strict checklist; you don't need to tick every box for delegation to happen. Often, you're balancing a mix of factors. You might not have someone who does not have the knowledge to do the task yet, but they're eager to learn. Or someone may be the ideal person, but they're currently at capacity. Or no one might be volunteering at all.

这些并不是一份严格的清单；你不必每一项都打勾才能开始授权。很多时候，你是在权衡一堆因素。你可能找不到一个已经具备所需知识的人，但他渴望学习。或者某个人是理想人选，但他目前已经满负荷。又或者，根本没有人主动站出来。

When no one steps up, try the following strategies to get people engaged.

当没有人站出来时，试试下面这些策略来让大家参与进来。

— PDF p.164 —

Ask directly, especially if you think someone is a strong fit: "I think you'd be great at this. How would you feel about taking it on?"

直接去问，尤其是当你觉得某个人很合适时："我觉得你做这件事会非常棒。你愿意接手吗？"

Connect it to their growth goals: "In your last review, we talked about building confidence through knowledge sharing. Want to run the next show-and-tell session?" Explain why you think it's a good opportunity and have an open conversation. If they hesitate, explore why. Maybe they're unsure how to start. Offer support by pairing with someone or doing a dry run.

把它和他们的成长目标联系起来："上次绩效沟通时，我们聊到要通过知识分享来建立自信。下一次 show-and-tell 分享会，你来主持怎么样？"解释你为什么认为这是个好机会，并和对方坦诚地谈一谈。如果他犹豫，去探究原因。也许他只是不知道该怎么开始。可以通过和别人结对、或先做一次彩排来提供支持。

Ask for help, with vulnerability: "I'm overloaded with this stakeholder presentation. Could you please prepare and run next week's product demo?" Being honest about your own challenges makes people more willing to step up.

带着脆弱去求助："这个给干系人的演示把我压得够呛。下周的产品 demo，能不能由你来准备并主持？"坦诚面对自己的难处，会让人们更愿意站出来帮忙。

Don't expect everyone to jump in. But one person might, and that's enough to start momentum. Often, delegation creates compounding effects. When others see peers take on new responsibilities and succeed, they're more likely to follow. Highlight these examples in one-on-ones to encourage others.

不要指望所有人都立刻跳出来。但只要有一个人愿意，就足以启动势头。授权往往会产生复利效应。当其他人看到同伴承担了新职责并取得成功时，他们更有可能跟上。在一对一里多强调这些例子，以鼓励更多人。

The tone of your ask matters. Avoid assigning or pressuring people into something they clearly don't want. Ownership can't be forced.

你开口时的语气很重要。不要强派、不要施压，尤其当对方明显不想要的时候。主人翁责任感是逼不出来的。

Still, if you've tried all this and the team continues to resist, that's likely pointing to a deeper issue. At that point, I'd bring it to a retrospective. Talk about the elephant in the room—the lack of engagement or willingness to take ownership—and work together to understand why. Whatever the reason, surfacing the issue is the first step to solving it.

不过，如果你这些都试过了，团队仍然抵触，那很可能指向一个更深层的问题。到那一步，我会把它拿到回顾会上谈。聊聊房间里那头大象——大家缺乏参与、不愿承担主人翁责任——并一起弄清楚为什么。无论原因是什么，把问题摆上台面，都是解决它的第一步。

Choosing the right person to delegate to takes intention, not perfection. There's no one-size-fits-all answer, just a mix of judgment, context, and experimentation. The more you practice, the better you'll get at reading the room, matching people with opportunities, and creating space for everyone to grow.

选对授权对象，靠的是用心，而不是完美。没有放之四海而皆准的答案，只有判断、情境与尝试的结合。你练习得越多，就越善于读懂局面、把人和机会匹配起来，并为每一个人创造成长的空间。

Choose the Right Delegation Strategy选择合适的授权策略

Delegation doesn't mean dumping your work onto someone else. You can't just hand off a task and expect it to be done perfectly without any guidance. Some people will need more support, some less. Your job is to provide the right level of direction based on the person's experience, skill level, and confidence with the task.

授权并不意味着把自己的工作一股脑倒给别人。你不能只是把任务一交，就指望它在没有任何指导的情况下被完美完成。有些人需要更多支持，有些人则少一些。你的工作，就是根据对方的经验、技能水平和对这项任务的信心，提供恰到好处的指导力度。

— PDF p.165 —

Once you've identified the right person, the actual handover begins. Start by explaining why you're choosing them for this task. Maybe it's because they've shown interest in the topic or because of their technical knowledge, their ability to think outside the box, or their strong collaboration skills. Whatever the reason, say it out loud. This helps set the right expectations and avoids misunderstandings like "Why am I getting more work?" or "Are they just throwing this on my plate because they don't want to do it?" If people understand why you're delegating something to them, they're more likely to approach it with the right mindset.

一旦选定了合适的人，真正的交接就开始了。先解释你为什么选他来做这件事。也许是因为他对这个主题表现出兴趣，也许是因为他的技术知识、跳出框架思考的能力，或是他出色的协作能力。无论原因是什么，都把它说出口。这有助于设定正确的期望，避免诸如"为什么活儿都堆到我头上？"或"他们是不是自己不想干，才把这个甩给我？"之类的误解。如果人们明白你为什么把这件事授权给他，他们就更可能以正确的心态去接手。

Of course, give them a chance to ask questions, raise concerns, or even push back if it's not something they feel ready for or interested in.

当然，也要给对方机会去提问、提出顾虑，甚至在他觉得自己没准备好或不感兴趣时表达反对。

Match delegation style to the situation让授权风格匹配情境

Not everyone needs the same level of support when taking on a task. The way you delegate should depend on the person's knowledge, experience, and confidence in handling it. Think of delegation as a spectrum, from high direction and hands-on support to full autonomy.

并非每个人在接手任务时都需要同等程度的支持。你授权的方式，应取决于对方的知识、经验以及他对处理这件事的信心。可以把授权想象成一个光谱：从高度指挥、手把手支持，一直到完全自主。

This approach is inspired by the Situational Leadership Model (originally developed by Hersey and Blanchard), which emphasizes adapting your leadership style to the development level of the person you're supporting.

这一思路借鉴了情境领导模型（Situational Leadership Model，最初由 Hersey 和 Blanchard 提出），其核心是：根据你所支持对象的发展阶段，灵活调整你的领导风格。

Here are four key approaches based on the person's situation:

下面是根据对方所处情境划分的四种关键方式：

Telling (directing)告知式（指挥）

This is for someone who has little to no experience with the task and may also be hesitant or unwilling to take it on. In this case, clear instructions and close guidance are necessary. Define the task step-by-step, explain exactly what's expected, and check in frequently to make sure they're on the right track.

这适用于那些对该任务几乎没有经验、并且可能犹豫不决或不愿接手的人。在这种情况下，清晰的指令和密切的指导是必要的。一步一步地定义任务、讲清楚到底期望什么，并频繁跟进，以确保他们走在正确的轨道上。

Example: A team member is preparing for their first client-facing demo. Instead of just handing over the calendar invite, help them understand the audience and their expectations, review the content together, and do a dry run where they can practice with you and get feedback. Attend the demo to offer backup if needed, and debrief together afterward.

例子：某位团队成员正在准备他第一次面向客户的演示。不要只是把日历邀请转给他，而要帮他理解听众是谁、听众有什么期望，一起过一遍内容，并做一次彩排——让他在你面前演练、并拿到反馈。如果需要，你到场为他兜底，结束后再一起复盘。

— PDF p.166 —

Selling (coaching)推销式（辅导）

This approach works when someone is eager to take on a task but lacks the skills or confidence to do it on their own. They might hesitate because they think they're not capable. Here, your job is to build their confidence while providing the necessary training and support.

这种方式适用于：一个人很想接手某项任务，但缺乏独立完成它所需的技能或信心。他可能因为觉得自己不行而犹豫。这时，你的工作是建立他的信心，同时提供必要的培训和支持。

Example: If a team member is interested in leading sprint planning but feels unsure, you could coach them through the process. Have them shadow you the first time, then let them lead the next session with your support, offering feedback and encouragement afterward.

例子：如果某位团队成员有兴趣主持冲刺计划会、但心里没底，你可以在过程中辅导他。第一次让他在旁边观摩你做，下一次则在你的支持下由他来主持，结束后再给予反馈和鼓励。

Participating (supporting)参与式（支持）

At this stage, the person has the skills and experience to perform the task but may benefit from occasional input, encouragement, or collaboration. The focus here is less on instruction and more on confidence-building, motivation, or being a sounding board. You take a more collaborative approach, supporting their decisions, removing blockers, and checking in as needed while allowing them to take the lead.

到了这个阶段，对方已经具备完成任务的技能和经验，但偶尔的建议、鼓励或协作仍会让他获益。此时重点不在于指挥，而在于建立信心、激励他，或做他的"回音壁"。你采取更协作的方式：支持他的决策、清除障碍，并按需跟进，同时让他来牵头。

Example: A developer who has previously worked on tech design documents together with you now wants to write one independently. Instead of reviewing every line, you provide feedback only if needed and encourage them to refine their approach. Finally, before the document is officially finalized, you might want to review it with them, ensuring alignment and making any necessary adjustments together, as the accountability remains with you as the tech lead.

例子：一位开发者以前和你一起做过技术设计文档，现在想独立写一份。你不必逐行审阅，而是只在需要时给出反馈，并鼓励他完善自己的思路。最后，在文档正式定稿之前，你可以和他一起过一遍，确保方向一致、共同做必要的调整——因为作为技术负责人，最终的担责仍在你身上。

Delegating (hands-off)授权式（放手）

When someone is fully capable and confident in handling a task, your job is to step back. Let them own it entirely while staying available if they need support.

当一个人完全有能力、也有信心处理某项任务时，你的工作就是退到后面。让他完全拥有这件事，同时保持在线，以备他需要支持时随时可找。

Example: A senior engineer has been leading technical discovery sessions for new projects. She is experienced in gathering requirements, assessing technical feasibility, and facilitating discussions with stakeholders. At this point, she doesn't need your guidance, just the space to do her job. You check in occasionally to offer support or remove blockers if needed, but you fully trust her to handle it independently.

例子：一位资深工程师一直在为新项目主持技术探索会议。她在收集需求、评估技术可行性、以及引导与干系人的讨论方面都很有经验。到这一步，她不需要你的指导，只需要做事的空间。你偶尔跟进一下，提供支持或在需要时清除障碍，但完全信任她能独立处理。

— PDF p.167 —

Adjust your delegation approach调整你的授权方式

People don't stay in one category forever. The goal is to help them move from needing a high amount of direction to full autonomy. If you're always in "telling mode" with a capable team, you'll be micromanaging. If you immediately take a hands-off approach with someone new to a task, they might feel abandoned and struggle.

人不会永远停留在某一个类别里。目标是帮助他们从需要大量指挥，一步步走向完全自主。如果你对一支有能力的团队始终停留在"告知模式"，那就是在微观管理。而如果你对一个刚接触某项任务的人立刻采取放手策略，他可能会觉得被抛弃，进而举步维艰。

A good rule of thumb is to start with more guidance and gradually pull back as the person builds confidence and skills. Effective delegation removes work from your plate while helping your team grow and ensuring tasks are completed successfully.

一条很好的经验法则是：从较多指导开始，随着对方信心和技能的建立，再逐步后撤。高效授权既能把工作从你肩上卸下，又能帮助团队成长，并确保任务被成功完成。

It's useful to mention that not everyone needs the same level of support for every task. One person might be highly autonomous when working on backend systems but need more direction when dealing with stakeholders. It's not about labeling people but about adapting your approach to each situation and skill set. Think of it as calibrating your support to match the task at hand.

有一点值得一提：并非每个人在每一项任务上都需要同等程度的支持。一个人在做后端系统时可能高度自主，但在和干系人打交道时却需要更多指引。这不是给人贴标签，而是根据具体情境和技能组合来调整你的方式。不妨把它想象成：校准你的支持力度，使之与手头的任务相匹配。

A great way to refine your delegation approach is by asking for feedback. After the task is completed, check in with them: how did they feel about the process? Did they get enough support? What could have been done differently? Their input will help you adjust your style and improve future delegations.

打磨授权方式的一个好办法，是主动征求反馈。任务完成后，和对方聊聊：他觉得整个过程如何？他得到的支持够不够？哪些地方本可以做得不一样？他的反馈会帮你调整风格，让以后的授权做得更好。

Effective delegation is about thoughtful adaptation. The more you tune into each person's experience and confidence level, the better you can support their growth and ensure successful outcomes.

高效授权，靠的是用心的灵活适配。你越能体察每个人的经验和信心水平，就越能支持他们成长、确保成功的结果。

Set Clear Expectations设定清晰的期望

"I'll just do it myself next time." If you've ever caught yourself thinking that after delegating a task, unclear expectations might be the real issue. Clear, up-front communication is what separates effective delegation from a frustrating cycle of rework and misalignment.

"下次我还不如自己做。"如果你在授权完一个任务后，心里冒出过这样的念头，那么真正的问题很可能出在期望不清晰。清晰、事前的沟通，正是把高效授权与那种令人沮丧的返工、错位循环区分开来的关键。

I remember this time when I asked a developer to prepare a showcase presentation. I thought it was obvious: prepare slides, do a demo, and get ready to present for five minutes like we usually do. I told her to ask me if she had any questions, have everything ready before the showcase, and leave some time for feedback. She didn't reach out during the preparation process, so I assumed things were going smoothly.

我记得有一次，我请一位开发者准备一场成果展示。我以为这是明摆着的事：准备幻灯片、做一个 demo、像往常那样准备好讲五分钟就行。我告诉她有问题就来问我，在展示前把一切准备妥当，并留出一些时间做反馈。准备过程中她没有来找我，于是我以为一切顺利。

— PDF p.168 —

Two hours before the showcase, I checked in to ask about the status, as I hadn't heard anything from her. She told me she had everything ready to go. Then, she showed up at the showcase with only one slide and one picture, which didn't take her longer than one minute to present. I was shocked. I definitely didn't react well at the moment. She didn't understand what she had done wrong, and to be honest, she was right. Because I never clearly told her what exactly I expected, I just assumed she knew.

展示开始前两小时，因为一直没她的消息，我主动去问进展。她告诉我一切都准备就绪。结果，她到了展示现场，只带了一页幻灯片和一张图，讲起来不到一分钟就说完了。我当时惊呆了。那一刻我的反应肯定很不好。她不明白自己错在哪里，而说实话，她确实没错——因为我从未清楚地告诉她我到底期望什么，我只是想当然地以为她知道。

That's when I learned a valuable lesson about the power of setting clear expectations when delegating. It's not enough to assume the other person understands. I needed to clearly communicate what I expected the outcome to be, define our roles in the process, explain how I'd know the task was done, and agree on all of this up front. After that experience, I made it a point to be much more specific about expectations whenever I delegated a task.

从那以后，我学到了宝贵的一课：授权时设定清晰期望的力量有多大。光想当然地认为对方理解是不够的。我需要清楚地讲清我期望的结果是什么、界定我们在这个过程中各自的角色、说明我怎么判断任务算完成，并把这一切在事先就达成一致。经历那件事之后，我给自己立了条规矩：以后每次授权任务，都要把期望说得具体得多。

That's also when I started leaning on a familiar framework: SMART goals. SMART goals aren't just for personal productivity; they're a powerful way to create alignment and accountability when delegating. They help ensure both sides are on the same page about what success looks like, what's expected, and when it should happen.

也正是在那时，我开始借助一个大家熟悉的框架：SMART 目标。SMART 目标不只用于个人效率；它也是授权时建立对齐与担责的有力工具。它能帮助双方在"成功长什么样、期望是什么、什么时候完成"这些问题上达成共识。

But over time, I realized something was missing. Delegation doesn't stop after the initial handoff; you also need a way to track how things are going. So I added one more T to the model: trackable. The result is a lightweight but powerful extension I use with my teams: SMARTT goals. Let's break it down:

但久而久之，我意识到还缺点什么。授权并不在初次交接后就结束；你还需要一种方式来跟踪事情进展如何。于是我在这个模型上又加了一个 T：可追踪（trackable）。于是就有了我在团队中使用的这套轻量却强大的扩展：SMARTT 目标。我们来逐条拆解：

Specific具体（Specific）

Be specific in outcome, flexible in execution. Be crystal clear about what the expected outcome is. If needed, provide some guidance on how you expect the task to be tackled, but keep in mind that the person taking it over should have the autonomy to decide the best approach. If the task requires collaboration, specify who else should be involved: team members, other teams, or even different departments. Also, share any relevant information you already have to give them a head start.

在结果上具体，在执行上灵活。把期望的结果讲得清清楚楚。如果需要，可以就你期望如何处理这项任务给出一些指导，但要记住：接手的人应该有自主决定最佳方式的权利。如果任务需要协作，指明还应让谁参与：团队成员、其他团队，甚至不同的部门。另外，把你已经掌握的相关信息分享出去，让他有一个好的起点。

— PDF p.169 —

Measurable可衡量（Measurable）

Define how success will be measured. This could be quantitative (e.g., reducing build time by 20%) or based on deliverables (e.g., producing a report with recommendations for improving system performance). Having a measurable goal helps track progress and ensures alignment.

定义成功将如何被衡量。它可以是量化的（例如：把构建时间缩短 20%），也可以基于交付物（例如：产出一份报告，其中包含改进系统性能的建议）。有一个可衡量的目标，有助于跟踪进展并确保对齐。

Achievable可实现（Achievable）

Is the goal realistic given the timeline and available resources? This is something you should discuss and agree on with the person taking over the task. If it's not achievable as originally planned, adjust accordingly.

考虑到时间线和可用资源，这个目标现实吗？这一点你应该和接手任务的人一起讨论、共同商定。如果按原计划无法实现，就相应地调整。

Relevant相关（Relevant）

Why does this task matter? Even if you think the purpose is obvious, take a moment to reiterate the "why." Understanding how their work contributes to the bigger picture will make them more engaged and invested in the task.

这项任务为什么重要？即便你觉得目的不言自明，也花点时间把"为什么"再讲一遍。让他们明白自己的工作如何服务于更大的图景，会让他们更投入、更上心。

Time-bound有时限（Time-bound）

Agree on a deadline. A clear timeline prevents tasks from dragging on indefinitely and helps the person prioritize effectively. Without this, things tend to get pushed to the bottom of the list, especially in busy teams.

商定一个截止日期。清晰的时间线能防止任务被无限期拖下去，并帮助对方有效地排优先级。没有这一点，事情往往会被推到清单最底部，尤其是在忙碌的团队里。

Trackable可追踪（Trackable）

How are you going to keep track of progress? Will it be on a Confluence board or a shared doc or via a regular check-in? How often will you review progress together to ensure things are on track? Having a clear system for tracking progress and checking in on progress significantly reduces the risk of unexpected surprises down the line.

你打算如何跟踪进展？是放在 Confluence 看板上、一份共享文档里，还是通过定期跟进？你们多久一起回顾一次进展，以确保事情走在正轨上？有一套清晰的跟踪和跟进机制，能显著降低日后出现意外状况的风险。

Table 6-1 shows an example of how you can apply SMARTT goals to a classic delegation scenario: delegate the initiative of reducing tech debt in your codebase to a senior engineer on your team.

表 6-1 展示了一个例子，说明如何把 SMARTT 目标应用到一个经典的授权场景中：把"减少代码库技术债"这一举措，授权给团队里的一位资深工程师。

By setting clear expectations like this, you significantly reduce the risk of misunderstandings, misalignment, and disappointing outcomes. When both you and the person you delegate to are on the same page from the start, it increases the likelihood of success and makes delegation a much smoother process.

通过像这样设定清晰的期望，你能大幅降低误解、错位和结果令人失望的风险。当你和被授权者从一开始就处在同一页上，成功的概率就会提高，授权过程也会顺畅得多。

— PDF p.170 —

Table 6-1. Example scenario using SMARTT goals

表 6-1. 使用 SMARTT 目标的示例场景

SMARTTSuggestions / 建议Example: delegate the initiative of reducing tech debt in your codebase to a senior dev in your team.示例：把“减少代码库技术债”这一举措，授权给团队里的一位资深开发者。
Specific / 具体What are the expected results? Who should be involved? Provide all relevant information you have about the task.期望的结果是什么？应该让谁参与？把你掌握的关于该任务的所有相关信息都提供出来。You are responsible for leading the initiative to address and reduce technical debt within our codebase. This includes:
• Reviewing the current list of technical debt tasks
• Working with the team to identify areas of high technical debt
• Prioritizing them based on impact and urgency
• Creating a detailed plan for addressing these issues
• Ensuring the team is following the plan 你负责牵头推进一项举措，在我们的代码库中处理并减少技术债。具体包括：
• 审阅现有的技术债任务清单
• 与团队一起识别技术债集中的区域
• 根据影响和紧急程度对它们排优先级
• 制定一份处理这些问题的详细计划
• 确保团队按计划执行
Measurable / 可衡量Quantities/deliverables.量化指标 / 交付物。The goal is to address 30% of technical debt tasks over the next three months. 目标是在接下来三个月内处理掉 30% 的技术债任务。
Achievable / 可实现Can the objective really be accomplished?这个目标真的能够完成吗？This tech debt task will be addressed alongside regular feature development tasks, with dedicated time allocated in each sprint. 这项技术债工作将与常规的功能开发任务并行处理，并在每个冲刺中划出专门的时间。
Relevant / 相关What is the point of doing this task?做这件事的意义是什么？Reducing technical debt is critical for:
• Improving the long-term maintainability of our codebase
• Speeding up future development
• Reducing the occurrence of bugs
• Reducing onboarding time for new developers
This initiative aligns with our broader goal of ensuring product stability. 减少技术债至关重要，因为它能：
• 提升代码库长期的可维护性
• 加快未来的开发速度
• 减少 bug 的出现
• 缩短新开发者的上手时间
这项举措与我们"保障产品稳定性"这一更宏观的目标相一致。
Time-bound / 有时限Clear timelines.清晰的时间线。This initiative should be completed within three months. 这项举措应在三个月内完成。
Trackable / 可追踪How will progress be monitored or reviewed?进展将如何被监控或回顾？• Progress will be tracked in a shared Confluence page, updated weekly with completed tasks and blockers.
• We'll review the status together during our Monday check-in meetings to ensure we're on track, and adjust if needed.
• The plan and updates will also be visible to the whole team for transparency. • 进展将在一个共享的 Confluence 页面上跟踪，每周更新已完成的任务和阻塞项。
• 我们会在每周一的跟进会上一起回顾状态，确保走在正轨上，并在需要时调整。
• 计划和更新对整个团队可见，以保持透明。
— PDF p.171 —

Follow Up跟进

Once a task is completed, regardless of the outcome, following up is essential. It supports your team's growth and helps you refine your leadership approach.

任务一旦完成，无论结果如何，跟进都是必不可少的。它支持团队的成长，也帮你打磨自己的领导方式。

Share your feedback on how the process went, looking at both the final result and how things went overall with the person you delegated to:

和被授权者一起，既看最终结果、也看整个过程，分享你对这次过程的反馈：

  • What worked well?哪些地方做得好？
  • What challenges did they face?他们遇到了哪些挑战？
  • What could be done better next time?下次哪些地方可以做得更好？

Make sure to ask them for their feedback too. A simple but powerful question like "What could I have done differently to support you better in this process?" keeps delegation iterative and continuously improving, making it easier for both you and your team to refine how you work together over time.

也一定要向对方征求反馈。一个简单却有力的问题——"在这个过程中，我本可以做些什么不同的事，来更好地支持你？"——能让授权成为一个不断迭代、持续改进的过程，让你和团队随着时间推移，更容易打磨彼此协作的方式。

Follow-ups also help validate your perspective on how things went, because sometimes, what you think happened and what the other person experienced can be completely different. Here's an example: a tech lead delegated the task of documenting the deployment process to another developer in the team. The goal was to get a high-level view of all the steps involved so the team could later discuss and identify blockers or areas for improvement. The tech lead also asked that the document be created in Confluence, since that was the team's standard documentation tool.

跟进还能帮你验证自己对过程的判断，因为有时你以为发生的事，和对方实际经历的事，可能完全是两回事。举个例子：一位技术负责人把"记录部署流程"这项任务授权给团队里另一位开发者。目标是获得一个关于所有相关步骤的高层视图，以便团队之后讨论、识别阻塞点或可改进之处。技术负责人还要求文档建在 Confluence 上，因为那是团队标准的文档工具。

The final result was great. The tech lead was happy with the work and assumed the other developer was too. But when they had the follow-up conversation, he was surprised to hear "I would have preferred using a better tool for building the diagram instead of Confluence, something more interactive."

最终结果很不错。技术负责人对这份工作很满意，并以为另一位开发者也一样。但在跟进谈话时，他惊讶地听到对方说："我本来更想用一个比 Confluence 更好用的工具来画这张图，用一个更具交互性的东西。"

Turns out, while the other developer did the task as requested, she was a little frustrated with the process but didn't say anything at the time. The tech lead realized he had been unnecessarily rigid about the tool choice. He wasn't even aware that this had caused friction until the follow-up chat.

原来，尽管那位开发者按要求完成了任务，她对这个过程却有点沮丧，只是当时没说。技术负责人这才意识到，自己在工具选择上不必要地死板了。直到这次跟进谈话，他才知道这造成了摩擦。

As you can see from the previous example, delegation doesn't end when the task is done. Following up is an opportunity for growth and refinement, both for the person you delegated to and for yourself. It ensures that delegation remains a learning process rather than just a one-time transfer of responsibility.

正如上面这个例子所示，授权并不在任务完成时就结束。跟进是一次成长和打磨的机会——无论是对被授权者，还是对你自己。它确保授权始终是一个学习过程，而不只是一次性的责任转移。

Stay Accountable保持担责

Delegation is the process of assigning tasks or responsibilities to others while maintaining accountability for the outcome. This means that, as a tech lead,

授权，是把任务或职责分派给他人、同时自己仍对最终结果保持担责的过程。这意味着，作为技术负责人，

— PDF p.172 —

even when you delegate a task to someone on your team, you are still the one stakeholders will turn to if things go wrong. You don't get to say, "Well, that was someone else's responsibility." Just as you get credit for your team's successes, you also take ownership of its failures.

即便你把一项任务授权给了团队里的某个人，一旦出了问题，干系人找到的仍然是你。你不能说："那是别人的责任。"正如团队的成功会记在你头上，团队的失败也同样由你来承担。

This is where the difference between accountability and responsibility becomes important:

这里，"担责（accountability）"与"负责（responsibility）"之间的区别就变得重要起来：

  • Responsibility means taking ownership of the work.负责，是对工作本身拥有主人翁感。
  • Accountability means taking ownership of the outcome.担责，是对最终结果拥有主人翁感。

A tech lead is accountable for the team's outcomes, while the whole team is responsible for executing the work. Think of it this way: when things go south, the tech lead is the first one in the line of fire. That's why effective delegation isn't just about handing off tasks; it's about ensuring that the work is done right, without micromanaging.

技术负责人对团队的结果担责，而整个团队对执行工作负责。可以这样理解：当事情出岔子时，技术负责人是第一个站在火线上的人。正因如此，高效授权不只是把任务交出去那么简单；它关乎在不微观管理的前提下，确保工作被正确地完成。

Being accountable also means you can't suddenly offload your entire plate and expect everything to run smoothly. You can't just toss tasks at people and walk away. You have to support them in delivering it well. It's a balance; you need to delegate enough to empower others without disappearing from the process.

担责还意味着：你不能突然把肩上的事一股脑卸掉，就指望一切照常运转。你不能把任务往人身上一扔就走人。你必须支持他们把事情做好。这是一种平衡：你既要授权到位、赋能他人，又不能从这个过程中彻底消失。

If you start throwing things into people's laps, not only will your team likely grow frustrated, but the work itself might suffer. And since you're still accountable for the outcome, it could easily backfire on you. Like you've seen throughout this chapter, even if you're not doing the task yourself, successful delegation still takes effort and intentionality. Start small by delegating one task at a time, so you can build trust, learn what works, and grow your confidence along the way.

如果你开始把事情劈头盖脸地砸给别人，团队很可能会越来越沮丧，工作本身也可能受损。而既然你仍对结果担责，这很容易反过来害到你自己。正如你在整章里看到的：即便任务不是你亲手做的，成功的授权仍然需要付出努力、需要用心。从一次只授权一个任务这种小事做起，这样你才能建立信任、摸索出有效做法，并在过程中积累自信。

The key to maintaining accountability while delegating is to create a clear feedback loop. Regular check-ins, structured updates, and clear expectations (as I cover in the section "Set Clear Expectations" on page 151) help them do a great job.

在授权的同时保持担责的关键，是建立一条清晰的反馈回路。定期跟进、结构化的进展汇报，以及清晰的期望（如我在第 151 页"设定清晰的期望"一节所讲），都能帮助对方把工作做好。

Of course, even with all of these practices in place, delegation still carries some risks. You can never control everything, especially when it comes to people. Tasks may get deprioritized, misunderstandings can happen, or someone might not deliver to the level you expected. You might realize too late that the person didn't feel comfortable asking for help. These things happen.

当然，即便有了这一整套做法，授权依然伴随着一些风险。你永远无法控制一切，尤其是在人这件事上。任务可能被降低优先级，误解可能发生，或者某人交付的水平可能达不到你的预期。你可能为时已晚地才意识到：对方当初并不好意思开口求助。这些情况都会发生。

So, even though these steps aren't a guarantee that everything will go perfectly, they significantly reduce the chances of things going wrong. And even

所以，尽管这些步骤并不能保证一切都完美无缺，它们却能显著降低出问题的概率。而且即便

— PDF p.173 —

when things do go wrong, you can recover. What's far riskier is trying to do it all yourself: that's the path to burnout, bottlenecks, and a team that never grows.

真的出了问题，你也能挽回。真正风险大得多的，是试图事事亲为：那通向的是倦怠、瓶颈，以及一支永远长不大的团队。

Mastering delegation means being intentional at every stage. From deciding what to delegate and to whom, to adjusting your style based on the situation, setting clear expectations, and following through with accountability, each step plays a role in making delegation really work.

精通授权，意味着在每一个阶段都用心。从决定授权什么、授权给谁，到根据情境调整风格、设定清晰期望，并以担责的态度贯彻到底——每一步都在让授权真正奏效中扮演着角色。

Why Tech Leads Struggle to Delegate and How to Overcome It技术负责人为何难以授权，以及如何克服

Some tech leads feel constantly overwhelmed, juggling too many things at once: coding, one-on-ones, alignment conversations, and putting out fires, all while trying to keep up with strategic initiatives. And despite working long hours and being in endless meetings, there are always more things they know are important but never get around to. They feel like their days slip away, running from one task to another, without ever having time to step back and plan.

有些技术负责人总觉得不堪重负，同时应付着太多事：写代码、一对一、对齐谈话、四处救火，同时还得努力跟上各项战略举措。尽管长时间工作、没完没了地开会，他们心里清楚重要的事还有一大堆，却永远挤不出时间去做。他们觉得日子在指间溜走，从一个任务扑到另一个，却从来没有时间退一步做规划。

Yet, even when it's obvious they need to offload work, they still hesitate to delegate. Why? Because deep down, they're afraid: afraid that the outcome won't be as good as if they did it themselves, afraid of not getting credit, afraid of the effort required to teach someone else, and ultimately, afraid of losing control.

然而，即便明摆着他们需要把工作卸出去，他们在授权时仍然犹豫。为什么？因为在内心深处，他们害怕：害怕结果不如自己动手做的好，害怕功劳被拿走，害怕教别人要付出的精力，以及归根结底——害怕失去控制。

The reality is that the main reason tech leads start delegating isn't because they want to; it's because they have to. Eventually, it just becomes impossible not to.

现实是：技术负责人开始授权，主要原因往往不是他们"想"，而是他们"不得不"。终有一天，不这么做已经不可能了。

This struggle is completely normal, especially for tech leads transitioning from an individual contributor role. As ICs, they were used to full ownership: knowing every detail of their work, delivering high-quality outcomes, and receiving direct recognition for it. Now, suddenly, success is no longer about what they personally deliver but about what their team delivers. That shift is not easy, but there is no way around it, as great leadership is about scaling impact.

这种挣扎完全正常，尤其是对于刚从个人贡献者角色转过来的技术负责人。做 IC 时，他们习惯了完全的主人翁感：了解自己工作的每一个细节、交付高质量的成果，并因此直接获得认可。而现在，突然之间，成功不再取决于他们个人交付了什么，而是取决于团队交付了什么。这个转变并不容易，但它绕不过去——因为卓越的领导力，本质上就是放大影响力。

In this section, I'll dive deep into the most common fears tech leads have around delegation, exploring practical ways to overcome them. The goal is to help you ease into delegation with more confidence, so you can reclaim your time, grow your team (and yourself), and ultimately improve overall team performance.

在本节中，我会深入探讨技术负责人在授权时最常见的几种恐惧，并探索克服它们的切实方法。目标是帮你更有信心地逐步进入授权状态，从而赢回时间、培养团队（以及你自己），并最终提升团队的整体绩效。

Afraid of Losing Control害怕失去控制

Delegation means enabling others to do the work, which is often harder than just doing it yourself because it requires you to let go of control.

授权意味着赋能他人去做这件事，而这往往比你自己动手更难——因为它要求你放下控制。

Most tech leads struggle with this, especially in the beginning. They're used to having full ownership over their own work as individual contributors in the team, knowing every detail, and being in control of outcomes. When they step

大多数技术负责人在这一点上都会挣扎，尤其是在刚开始的时候。他们做团队里的个人贡献者时，习惯了对自己的工作完全主人翁、了如指掌，并牢牢掌控结果。当他们走进

— PDF p.174 —

into a leadership role, they try to maintain that same level of control across the entire team. This often leads to micromanaging: reviewing every PR, being part of every decision, attending every team conversation. Many tech leads have tried this, but it's just not sustainable. Eventually, they burn out.

领导角色时，他们试图对整个团队维持同等程度的控制。这往往导致微观管理：审阅每一个 PR、参与每一个决策、参加每一次团队讨论。很多技术负责人都试过这条路，但它根本不可持续。最终，他们倦怠了。

And the worst part is that no matter how much effort you put into controlling everything, you're never truly in control. There are too many moving parts, too many variables that can shift unexpectedly. Trying to control everything creates frustration, both for you and your team. You feel like things are slipping through the cracks despite your best efforts, and in response, you try to control even more, trapping yourself in a cycle. The only way to break free from this loop is to accept that you can't control every little detail. What you can do is prepare for uncertainty and learn how to navigate things when they don't go as planned. That's what experienced tech leads continuously try to do.

而最糟糕的是：无论你花多大力气去控制一切，你都永远无法真正掌控。变动的环节太多，意外变化的变量也太多。试图控制一切，会让你和团队都感到挫败。你觉得自己已经尽了最大努力，事情却仍在缝隙里溜走，于是你反过来试图控制得更多，把自己困在一个循环里。打破这个循环的唯一办法，就是接受"你无法控制每一个细节"。你能做的，是为不确定性做好准备，并学会在事情不按计划发展时如何应对。这正是有经验的技术负责人一直在努力做的事。

At the root of most delegation struggles, whether it's worrying about the outcome, thinking "it's quicker and easier to just do it myself," or even fearing that you won't get the credit, lies the fear of losing control. It's the biggest mental challenge tech leads face when letting go.

在大多数授权挣扎的根源——无论是担心结果、觉得"自己做更快更省事"，还是害怕功劳落不到自己头上——底下，都埋着对失去控制的恐惧。它是技术负责人在放手时面临的最大心理挑战。

This fear is especially strong because delegation requires vulnerability. It means trusting others with responsibilities you used to own. In leadership, vulnerability is often misunderstood as a weakness, when in fact, it's one of the greatest strengths of a successful tech lead, and a powerful way to build trust.

这种恐惧尤其强烈，因为授权需要你展露脆弱。它意味着把你曾经亲手承担的责任，交托给别人。在领导力中，"脆弱"常常被误解为软弱，而事实上，它恰恰是成功技术负责人最伟大的力量之一，也是建立信任的有力方式。

If you want your team to trust you, you need to trust them. Struggling to let go is often a sign of distrust: worrying that they will drop the ball, that they won't do the task as well as you, that things won't turn out exactly how you want. And if you don't know what your team is capable of, that fear makes sense. But the only way to find out is to take chances on people, give them opportunities to prove themselves. You might be surprised at what they can do when given the space to own a task.

如果你想让团队信任你，你就得先信任他们。难以放手，往往是不信任的表现：担心他们会把球掉在地上、担心他们做不到你那么好、担心结果不会完全如你所愿。而如果你并不了解团队的能力边界，这种恐惧是可以理解的。但要弄清楚，唯一的办法就是在人身上下注，给他们证明自己的机会。当你给人空间去拥有一个任务时，他们能做到的事可能会让你惊讶。

So, I invite you to try. The best way to start overcoming the fear of losing control is to practice delegation in small steps. You don't have to hand off everything at once, and there are ways to do so without micromanaging. The secret is slow exposure: start with a low-risk task, set clear expectations, and check in without hovering. By applying the strategies from the section "Delegation Process: Step-by-Step" on page 143, setting clear expectations, having a transparent tracking process, and understanding your role in delegation, you can maintain visibility without needing to be involved in every step.

所以，我邀请你试一试。克服对失去控制的恐惧，最好的起步方式就是小步练习授权。你不必一下子把所有事都交出去，而且也有办法在不微观管理的前提下做到。秘诀是"缓慢暴露"：从一个低风险任务开始，设定清晰的期望，跟进但不要 hovering（悬在头顶盯着）。通过运用第 143 页"授权流程：一步一步来"一节中的策略、设定清晰期望、建立透明的跟踪过程，并理解你在授权中的角色，你可以保持对局面的可见度，而不必介入每一个步骤。

— PDF p.175 —

A simple task to start with is asking someone else to facilitate the daily standup. This is a common action that tech leads, focused on control, do to ensure they are getting all the necessary updates and information to stay up-to-date with everything that is happening, often saying, "No one else will do it if I don't." But the opposite can be true too: no one else jumps in because they know you are always the one doing it. So, try telling your team that you'd like to mix it up a bit, and ask who would like to take over or come up with a plan for a rotation process. This might be an easy way to start exploring delegation since you're still part of those conversations. You can continue asking the questions you need to ask and make sure you get the information, even if you're not the one facilitating. Plus, the chances of things going completely sideways are smaller because they've seen you run it for a while now.

一个可以立刻开始的简单任务，是请别人来主持每日站会。技术负责人因为执着于控制，常常亲自主持站会，以确保自己拿到所有必要的更新和信息、对正在发生的一切了如指掌，还常说："我不做的话，没人会做。"但反过来也成立：没有人站出来接，是因为他们知道这事永远是你在做。所以，不妨告诉团队你想换个方式，问问谁愿意接手，或者一起设计一个轮流主持的方案。这也许是探索授权的一个轻松入口，因为你仍然是这些对话的参与者。你可以继续提出你需要问的问题，确保自己拿到信息，即便主持的人不是你。此外，事情彻底跑偏的概率也更小——毕竟大家已经看你主持好一阵子了。

Once you agree on a process for facilitation, set some ground rules. For example: we go over the board left to right (Backlog → To Do → In Progress → In Review → Testing → Done), discussing progress and potential blockers with the goal of going through all the tasks within the reserved time, leaving a few minutes at the end for announcements like "I have a medical appointment from 3 to 4, so I will not be available." Say the things that sound obvious; those are the ones that generate the most misunderstanding and conflicts in the team. Also, keep in mind that this is a continuous process. If you feel something isn't being addressed correctly, you can always discuss it with your team or give individual feedback.

一旦就主持流程达成一致，就定一些基本规则。例如：我们从左到右过看板（Backlog → To Do → In Progress → In Review → Testing → Done），讨论进展和潜在阻塞，目标是在预留时间内过完全部任务，并在最后留几分钟做公告，比如"我三点到四点有个医疗预约，届时不在"。把那些听起来不言而喻的事也讲出来；恰恰是这些事，最容易在团队里造成误解和冲突。另外要记住，这是一个持续的过程。如果你觉得有什么没被正确处理，随时可以和团队讨论，或给出一对一的反馈。

The same applies when handling urgent bugs reported by clients. Instead of taking the lead and verifying what is happening yourself, agree on a process with your team to handle them together, perhaps by rotating people, for example. To help you feel more in control at first, you can ask them to escalate to you if there's a bigger problem or if they can't handle it within a certain time threshold.

处理客户报来的紧急 bug 时也是同理。不要自己冲上去牵头、亲自去核实发生了什么，而是和团队约定一个流程，一起处理它们——比如通过轮流的方式。为了让你一开始更有掌控感，你可以要求他们：如果遇到更大的问题、或在某个时间阈值内处理不了，就升级上报给你。

Sometimes, losing control is exactly what needs to happen. When you give people ownership, they bring fresh ideas and approaches you may not have considered. It will also help you develop resilience and learn how to deal with things when they go wrong.

有时候，"失去控制"恰恰是必须发生的事。当你把主人翁感交给人们时，他们会带来你从未想到过的新鲜想法和做法。这也会帮你培养韧性，学会在事情出岔子时如何应对。

I can say from experience that once you experience the benefits of letting go of control, you won't want to go back. I started off as a micromanager and burned out one month into the role. But I learned to do better, and delegation was a game-changer.

凭经验我可以说：一旦你尝到了放下控制的甜头，就再也不想回头了。我一开始是个微观管理者，上任一个月就倦怠了。但我学会了做得更好，而授权彻底改变了局面。

Over time, you'll see that letting go doesn't mean losing control. It means gaining a stronger, more capable team. By embracing vulnerability and letting

久而久之你会发现，放手并不意味着失去控制。它意味着收获一支更强大、更能干的团队。通过拥抱脆弱、放下

— PDF p.176 —

go of control, you'll scale your positive impact as a leader in tech: you'll create growth opportunities for your team members, and both they and you will learn and grow together.

控制，你将放大作为技术领导者的正面影响力：你会为团队成员创造成长机会，而他们和你都将一同学习、一同成长。

Worried About the Outcome担心结果不够好

The second common fear tech leads have when delegating is worrying about the outcome of the delegated task not being as good as if they did it themselves.

技术负责人在授权时第二种常见的恐惧，是担心被授权任务的结果，不如自己动手做得好。

This can be addressed by setting clear expectations.

这个问题可以通过设定清晰的期望来解决。

I remember when I was talking to another tech lead about a situation he had gone through. He had delegated the task of writing technical documentation for a new feature to one of his team members. He had originally planned to do it himself but, like many of us, got overwhelmed with other tasks. So, he decided to ask a team member to handle it instead.

我记得曾和另一位技术负责人聊起他经历过的一件事。他把"为一个新功能撰写技术文档"的任务授权给了团队里的一名成员。他原本打算自己写，但和我们很多人一样，被其他任务压得喘不过气。于是，他决定请一位团队成员来处理。

He gave the person a vague instruction: "Please write up the documentation for the new feature so the team can understand how it works." He didn't specify things like the format, the level of detail, or even if things like code examples, diagrams, or edge cases were necessary. He assumed that the team member knew what was expected, based on the way other technical documents had looked before.

他给对方的指示很含糊："请为这个新功能写好文档，好让团队明白它是怎么工作的。"他没有说明格式、详细程度，甚至没有讲清楚是否需要代码示例、图表或边界情况之类的东西。他想当然地以为：基于以前那些技术文档的样子，这位成员知道该写成什么样。

A day later than expected, the documentation came in. But when he reviewed it, he was disappointed. It was just a brief overview, explaining what the feature did, but it lacked real depth. There were no architectural diagrams, no edge case handling, and no detailed explanations that would have made it helpful for the team. It was functional, but far from what he needed. In the end, he ended up spending more time updating and fixing the documentation than he would have if he had just written it himself from scratch.

比预期晚了一天，文档交了上来。但他一看，很失望。那只是一份简短的概述，解释了功能做什么，却缺乏真正的深度。没有架构图、没有边界情况处理，也没有那些本会让文档对团队真正有用的详细说明。它能用，却远不是他需要的。最后，他花在修改和补全这份文档上的时间，比自己从头写还要多。

He shared with me how frustrated he was, but as we discussed it, he realized he was partly to blame. He hadn't set clear expectations from the start. He hadn't explicitly stated what level of detail was needed, who the documentation was for (developers, QA, or nontechnical people), or even the key components like code examples, error handling, or diagrams.

他和我倾诉自己有多沮丧，但在我们讨论的过程中，他意识到自己也要负一部分责任。他从一开始就没有设定清晰的期望。他没有明确说明需要多详细、这份文档是给谁看的（开发者、QA，还是非技术人员），甚至没有讲清楚代码示例、错误处理或图表这些关键组成部分。

When he reflected on it and talked about it with another colleague, he came to the conclusion that, had he set proper expectations, this could have been avoided. The next time he delegated a similar task, he was much more specific about what he expected, and the outcome was completely different.

当他反思这件事、并和另一位同事聊起时，他得出结论：如果当初设定了恰当的期望，这件事本可以避免。下一次授权类似任务时，他对自己的期望具体得多，结果也完全不同。

This is a common story I hear from tech leads, and it's a great example of how important it is to be clear and specific when delegating tasks, especially something like documentation, where the format, level of detail, and intended

这是我从技术负责人那里听到的一个常见故事，它很好地说明了：授权任务时清晰、具体有多么重要——尤其是像文档这种，其格式、详细程度和目标

— PDF p.177 —

audience can really affect how useful the end result is. (More on this in the section "Set Clear Expectations" on page 151.)

读者会实实在在影响最终成果实用性的事情。（详见第 151 页"设定清晰的期望"一节。）

Giving very specific instructions is a way to ease into the process of delegation and get more comfortable with it. But it shouldn't always be your default strategy. As you get more into the habit of delegation and gain more trust in your team members, your guidelines should become more high-level. Focus on what the outcome should be, share the information you already have on the task, agree on a timeline, and leave the rest to them. Give them more autonomy to figure out how to address the task, who to talk to, and how to approach the solution. You might be surprised by how people can positively surprise you when given the chance.

给出非常具体的指示，是一种逐步进入授权过程、让自己更适应它的方式。但它不应永远是你的默认策略。随着你越来越养成授权的习惯、越来越信任团队成员，你的指导应该变得更宏观。聚焦于结果应该是什么，分享你已经掌握的关于任务的信息，商定一个时间线，其余的就交给他们。给他们更多自主权，去琢磨如何处理任务、该和谁沟通、以及如何着手解决。只要给人们机会，他们带来的正向惊喜可能会让你意外。

When you give others the space to add their own touch to a task, they often come up with better solutions than you might have. They have a more objective view of the problem or maybe a different experience to draw from. A lot of great things can come from letting people put their own spin on the task. They're more motivated because they can get creative, instead of just following a list of steps, and the solution they come up with could be even better than yours, ultimately benefiting the entire team. And keep in mind that whatever good work your team produces reflects positively on you as a tech lead. This has happened to me.

当你给别人空间在任务里加入自己的印记时，他们往往能想出比你更好的解决方案。他们对问题的视角更客观，或者有不同的经验可以借鉴。让人们给任务加上自己的诠释，往往能催生很多好东西。他们更有动力，因为可以发挥创意，而不只是照着一张步骤清单走；而他们想出的方案甚至可能比你的更好，最终让整个团队受益。还要记住：团队产出的任何优秀成果，都会正面地反映到你这位技术负责人身上。这种事就发生在我身上过。

There was a time when I delegated a complex task of optimizing a performance bottleneck in our application. I had initially thought of a solution that I thought would be the best approach, but one of the developers on my team came up with an alternative method. She suggested a faster, more efficient solution that was more streamlined than my own idea. After reviewing it, I realized that her approach was not only faster but also easier to implement with fewer changes to the existing codebase. The result was a performance boost that exceeded our expectations in both speed and stability, and she felt more empowered because she was able to take ownership of the solution. It made me realize that sometimes stepping back and trusting the team can lead to even better outcomes than I had initially anticipated.

有一次，我把一个复杂任务——优化我们应用中的一个性能瓶颈——授权了出去。我最初想到了一个自认为最佳的方案，但团队里一位开发者提出了另一种方法。她建议了一个更快、更高效的方案，比我自己的思路更精简。我评审之后发现，她的方法不仅更快，而且更容易实现，对现有代码库的改动也更少。结果是一次性能提升，在速度和稳定性两方面都超出了我们的预期；而她因为能拥有这个解决方案，也感到更有力量。这让我意识到：有时退一步、信任团队，带来的结果甚至会比我最初预想的更好。

This brings me to the point that while delegation starts with providing clear expectations, it also grows into empowering your team. Trusting them with autonomy can lead to great things.

这就引出了我的观点：授权始于提供清晰的期望，但它会成长为对团队的赋能。把自主权信任地交到他们手上，往往能成就了不起的事。

“It’s Quicker and Easier to Just Do It Myself”“自己做更快更省事”

As a tech lead, there's always that one task you've been doing for what feels like forever because you know how to do it best. Maybe it's debugging the CI/CD pipeline when it fails, because you've been in the team the longest, were there

作为技术负责人，总有那么一个任务，你感觉自己做了好久好久，因为你知道自己最擅长做它。也许是在 CI/CD 流水线挂掉时去调试它——因为你在团队里资历最老、从它刚搭建时就在场、

— PDF p.178 —

when it was first set up, and know all its moving parts. You've done it a dozen times, it doesn't break often, and fixing it usually takes only 15 minutes. It's easier to just take care of it yourself rather than delegate it to someone else. It's a scenario most of us have been in: feeling like it'll just take too long to explain to someone else, and you can knock it out in half the time.

清楚它所有的运转部件。你已经做过十几次，它不常坏，修起来通常只要 15 分钟。与其授权给别人，不如自己动手搞定更省事。这是我们大多数人都经历过的场景：觉得给别人解释太费时间，而你自己一半时间就能搞定。

But that 15-minute fix comes at a cost. Every time something breaks, it derails your day. Beyond the disruption, context switching, and handling something that could easily be done by someone else in the team, you are also putting your team at risk. If the issue happens while you're on vacation, out sick, or just unavailable, your team is blocked from deploying. They're stuck, unsure where to start, and delivery stalls. Also, by always being the one to jump in and fix it, you're creating a knowledge silo; no one else gets the chance to learn the process or improve upon it.

但那 15 分钟的修复是有代价的。每次东西一坏，就把你一整天的节奏带偏。除了被打断、上下文切换、以及处理一件团队里别人本可以轻松搞定的事之外，你还把团队置于风险之中。如果问题发生在你度假、生病或正好没空的时候，你的团队就被卡住、无法部署。他们僵在那里，不知从何下手，交付就此停滞。而且，因为永远是你跳出来修，你还在制造知识孤岛；其他人永远得不到学习这个流程、或改进它的机会。

Now, let's say you pass the task on to someone else. Here's how you could approach it.

现在，假设你把这个任务交给了别人。下面是你可以采取的做法。

During your next standup, say something like "I've been handling CI/CD issues when they pop up, but I'd like to teach someone else how to manage them. Who's interested?" You'll likely get a volunteer who's eager to grow in that area.

在下一次站会上，这样说："CI/CD 出问题时一直是我在处理，但我想教另一个人来管理它们。谁有兴趣？"你很可能会找到一个渴望在该领域成长的志愿者。

Alternatively, bring it up in a one-on-one. If you notice someone who's curious or looking for a new challenge, you might say: "I usually take care of this, but I think it's a great opportunity for you to learn. Want to pair on it this time?" That way, you're not just delegating a task; you're giving them space to grow and build confidence in a new skill.

或者，在一对一里提这件事。如果你注意到某个人很好奇、或在寻找新的挑战，你可以说："这事往常都是我来管，但我觉得对你来说会是个很好的学习机会。这次要不要和我一起做？"这样一来，你不只是在授权一个任务；你是在给对方空间去成长，并在一项新技能上建立自信。

Imagine next week, the issue comes up again. Instead of jumping in solo, you spend 30 minutes pairing with them to fix it, or better yet, record a walk-through or help them document the process.
